Demo: subscribe one listener to `cartCount` and one to `user`; then set an unrelated `user` patch, then `cartCount` 0 → 2, then `theme` (selected by nobody).

```bash
node solution.js
```


exercises.prompt:
Given a component tree (parent map) and a `reads` map of state variable → components that read it, compute where each variable should live: colocate in the sole reader, or lift to the lowest common ancestor of multiple readers. Log `<var>: read by <a>, <b> -> COLOCATE in <c> (...)` or `<var>: read by <a>, <b> -> LIFT to <c> (lowest common ancestor)`.

Tree: App → Header, SearchBar, Main, Footer; Main → Toolbar, DataTable, DetailPanel. Reads: query → [SearchBar]; sortBy → [Toolbar, DataTable]; selectedId → [DataTable, DetailPanel]; theme → [Header, Footer].

Run it:

```bash
node solution.js
```

Expected output (exactly):

```
query: read by SearchBar -> COLOCATE in SearchBar (only reader — no lifting needed)
sortBy: read by Toolbar, DataTable -> LIFT to Main (lowest common ancestor)
selectedId: read by DataTable, DetailPanel -> LIFT to Main (lowest common ancestor)
theme: read by Header, Footer -> LIFT to App (lowest common ancestor)
```
exercises.title: Colocation refactor planner

lessons.body:
## The rule

State lives as low as possible, and as high as necessary. Every piece of state should sit in the lowest component that (transitively) needs it — and no lower, no higher. Lifting is not a default; it is a response to a second reader.

## Symptoms of misplaced state

- State at the root that one leaf reads → every keystroke re-renders the app.
- Prop drilling through four layers for a single leaf → the state is either too high or wants context.
- Sibling A sets state that only sibling B reads → both should share a parent that owns it, nothing higher.

## The derived-state trap

Do not `useState` what you can compute during render. `fullName` derived from `firstName`/`lastName` is not state — it is a calculation. Storing derivations creates a second source of truth that drifts. If the derivation is expensive, `useMemo` it; the rule is about *storage*, not *recomputation*.

## URL as state

Filters, sort order, pagination, selected tabs — anything shareable — belong in the URL (query params). It survives refresh, works with the back button, and makes "link me to this view" free. Component state is for the ephemeral: form drafts, hover, open/closed.
keyPoints: State lives as low as possible, as high as necessary — lift only for a second reader.
Root-level state read by one leaf turns every update into a full-tree render.
Never store what you can derive during render; useMemo the expensive derivations.
Shareable UI state (filters, sort, page) belongs in the URL, not in useState.
lessons.title: Colocate: State Lives As Low As Possible

lessons.body:
## The provider pattern

`createContext` + `Provider` + `useContext` broadcasts a value to a subtree without prop drilling. It shines for values that change rarely: theme, locale, the authenticated user, static config.

## The re-render gotcha

Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes — and *identity* is the trigger. This is the classic footgun:

```jsx
<MyContext.Provider value={{ theme, toggleTheme }}>
```

That object literal is a new identity every render, so every consumer re-renders on every parent render, even when `theme` never changed. Fix: `useMemo` the value.

## Split contexts

When one context carries both slow-changing data and stable actions, split it: a data context and an actions context (dispatch identity is stable by nature). Consumers of each then re-render only when their half changes. This is the same instinct as the selector pattern, expressed with built-in tools.

## When context is the wrong tool

High-frequency updates — mouse position, scroll offsets, tickers — through context re-render every consumer on every tick. That is an external store's job (next lesson), not context's.
keyPoints: Context broadcasts to a subtree; every consumer re-renders on value change.
Object-literal provider values recreate identity each render — useMemo them.
Split data contexts from action contexts so consumers re-render independently.
High-frequency updates belong in an external store, not context.
lessons.title: Context and Its Re-render Gotcha

lessons.body:
## The pattern

Keep state outside React. Components subscribe with a selector; the store notifies a subscriber only when its selected slice changes. Three operations are the whole API: `getState`, `setState`, `subscribe`.

```js
// shape of the idea (no library)
const unsub = store.subscribe(
  (s) => s.cart.items.length, // selector: the slice this component cares about
  (count) => renderBadge(count) // listener: runs only when the slice changes
);
```

## Why selectors beat broadcast

Context broadcasts to every consumer; a selector store filters at the subscription. Ten components reading ten different slices, one slice updating → one component re-renders. That per-component bailout is what makes external stores scale where context degrades.

## useSyncExternalStore

React's built-in hook for this pattern takes `subscribe` and `getSnapshot`. The subtle rule: the snapshot must be cached and immutable between store updates, or concurrent rendering can tear — different components reading different versions of the same state mid-render.

## When a library earns its place

Cross-tree shared state with frequent updates, complex derived selectors, persistence or middleware needs. Until then, `useState` + colocation + split contexts carry most apps further than people expect.
lessons.comparisonNote: Java's Observer / PropertyChangeListener notifies every listener on every event, and each listener filters inside its own update() method. The selector pattern inverts that: the store runs your selector on each change and only calls you when your slice changed — the filtering moves from the listener into the subscription. Same decoupling, less wasted work.
keyPoints: External store = getState + setState + subscribe; state lives outside React.
Selectors filter at the subscription: only components whose slice changed re-render.
useSyncExternalStore snapshots must be cached/immutable or concurrent renders tear.
Reach for a library for frequent cross-tree updates, derived selectors, or middleware — not before.
lessons.title: External Stores: Subscribe and Selectors

lessons.body:
## Server state is a cache problem

Server state is a local copy of something owned elsewhere: stale by definition, asynchronous by nature, and usually needed by more than one component. Treating it like client state — a `useState` per component that fetched it — is how apps end up with five copies of the user, all disagreeing.

## The patterns that matter

- **Fetch-on-render with in-flight dedupe:** two components requesting the same URL share one network request.
- **Cache with TTL:** don't refetch what you just fetched.
- **Stale-while-revalidate:** show the cached copy instantly, refresh in the background. Back-navigation feels instant.
- **Background refetch:** on window focus or an interval for data that drifts.
- **Optimistic updates:** apply the mutation locally, roll back on failure. Great UX, real complexity — reserve for high-value interactions.

## Client state vs server state

Form input, selection, panel open/closed → client state (`useState`). Anything that came from a fetch → server state: cache it in one place, derive the rest. When you are unsure which kind a value is, ask: "if the server changed this, should my UI know?" Yes → server state.

## No library endorsement

Whether you hand-roll these behaviors (the cache exercise in this module, the data client in the capstone) or adopt a library later, these are the behaviors to demand. The patterns are the durable knowledge; any specific API is replaceable.
keyPoints: Server state is a cache of remote data: stale by definition, shared across components.
Core patterns: dedupe in-flight, TTL cache, stale-while-revalidate, background refetch.
Optimistic updates are high-value, high-complexity — use sparingly.
Client state = ephemeral UI; server state = anything a fetch owns. Sort every value into one bucket.
lessons.title: Server State Is a Cache Problem

tagline: Where state lives decides how fast your app feels — colocation, context splits, external stores, and treating server data like the cache it is.
